title: Trees
summary: Preorder, inorder, postorder, and level order, and what each order is for.

parts.rule: A tree is a connected acyclic hierarchy. Pick a traversal by what you need: preorder for copy-shaped work, inorder for sorted binary-search-tree walks, postorder for delete-shaped work, level order for breadth.
parts.why: Hierarchy shows up in filesystems, DOM-like structures, and recursive partitions. Naming the order shows you know which visit sequence matches the job.

body:
Rule. A tree is a connected acyclic hierarchy. Pick a traversal by what you need: preorder for copy-shaped work, inorder for sorted binary-search-tree walks, postorder for delete-shaped work, level order for breadth.

Why it matters. Hierarchy shows up in filesystems, DOM-like structures, and recursive partitions. Naming the order shows you know which visit sequence matches the job.

SAMPLE example. SAMPLE: print a binary tree by levels using a queue. That is level order. Separately, an inorder walk of a binary search tree emits keys ascending. Mixing those orders without saying why loses the interview thread.

When to use. Model hierarchical data as a tree when each node has one parent path. Choose BFS for distance in edges, DFS for path-shaped recursion, and explicit stacks when recursion depth is risky.

When to refuse. Refuse calling a cyclic graph a tree. Refuse inorder language on a structure that is not a binary search tree if sorted output was the promise. Refuse storing children in ways that hide the parent link the algorithm needs.
